t.3.8.1: To the delight of the Raghus, her husband, who had set out after taking leave of Sutīkṣṇa, Vaidehī spoke these words in an affectionate voice.
t.3.8.2: This great dharma is attained through a very subtle discipline, and here it can be won only by one who has turned away from the vice that is born of desire.
t.3.8.3: Three vices indeed arise here, born of desire: false speech is the chief among them, and heavier still than that are the other two, going to another man's wife and cruelty without enmity.
t.3.8.4: A false word has never been yours, nor will it ever be, O Rāghava; how then could there be in you the coveting of the wives of others, which destroys dharma?
t.3.8.5: And all that, O mighty-armed one, can be borne only by those who have conquered their senses; and I know, O handsome one, that your senses are under your control.
t.3.8.6: The third is this fierce one, the taking of others' lives without any enmity, which is done out of delusion, and that has now presented itself to you.
t.3.8.7: O hero, you have pledged to slay the rākṣasas in battle in order to protect the sages who dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest.
t.3.8.8: And this is the reason you have set out with your brother, bearing bow and arrows, for the forest renowned by the name Daṇḍakā.
t.3.8.9: Therefore, seeing you set out, my mind is troubled with anxiety; as I reflect upon your conduct, may what is beneficial and supremely good come to pass.
t.3.8.11: For you, bow and arrows in hand, have come to the forest with your brother; on seeing all the creatures that roam the forest, you might well expend some of your arrows on them.
t.3.8.13: Long ago, it is said, O mighty-armed one, there lived an ascetic, truthful in speech and pure, in a certain holy forest where beasts and birds took delight.
t.3.8.10: Indeed, O hero, this going toward the Daṇḍakas does not please me. I shall tell you the reason for it; let it be heard from me as I speak.
t.3.8.12: Here in this world, the bow of kṣatriyas and the fuel of fire alike, when kept close at hand, make their fiery power and strength blaze up intensely.
t.3.8.14: Then Indra, the lord of Śacī, wishing to create an obstacle to that very ascetic's austerity, came to the hermitage sword in hand, assuming the form of a warrior.
t.3.8.15: In that hermitage of his an excellent sword was placed; it was given, in the manner of a deposit held in trust, to the one who was steadfast in holy austerity.
t.3.8.17: Wherever he went to gather roots and fruits, he never went without that sword, intent on guarding what had been entrusted to him.
t.3.8.16: Having received that weapon, he, intent on guarding the deposit, kept roaming through the forest with it, upholding the trust placed in him.
t.3.8.18: Constantly carrying the weapon, that ascetic, rich in austerity, gradually made his own mind fierce, abandoning his resolve in penance.
t.3.8.19: Then that sage, delighting in violence, heedless and dragged down by unrighteousness, went to hell because of his constant association with that weapon.
t.3.8.20: Out of affection and deep respect I only remind you; I do not presume to instruct you. Such an intention should by no means be formed by you, holding your bow in hand.
t.3.8.21: You have resolved to slay the rākṣasas who dwell in Daṇḍaka, though there is no enmity between you; but I do not wish, O hero, that beings be slain when they have done no wrong.
t.3.8.22: For heroic kṣatriyas who dwell in the forests with self-restraint, this much alone is the task to be done with the bow: the protection of the afflicted.
t.3.8.24: Then, noble one, the mind becomes sullied through the constant handling of weapons. Only when you have gone back to Ayodhyā will you practise the dharma of a kṣatriya.
t.3.8.23: Where is the weapon, and where the forest? Where is the warrior's calling, and where asceticism? We have thrown these opposites together; let the dharma proper to this place be honored.
t.3.8.26: From dharma arises wealth, from dharma springs happiness; by dharma one obtains everything. This world has dharma as its essence.
t.3.8.25: But the joy of my mother-in-law and father-in-law would be unending if, having renounced the kingdom, you were to become a sage devoted to austerity.
t.3.8.27: Having diligently mortified the self through these various observances, the skillful attain dharma; happiness is not gained through happiness.
t.3.8.29: This has been spoken by me out of a woman's fickleness; who is able to teach you dharma? Having reflected with your intellect, together with your younger brother, do without delay whatever pleases you.
t.3.8.28: O gentle one, pure-minded, always practice dharma in this forest of austerities; for everything is known to you, even the three worlds, in their true nature.
